target: AG1's claim that AI is broadly good for society because it improves convenience, health, accessibility, safety, productivity, and learning
objection: AI's apparent benefits are outweighed by harms in practice: it can displace workers, reduce wages, create fragile gig-style work, and leave productivity gains unevenly shared, harming the economic well-being of many people and businesses.

target: AG1's assumption that AI helps students and professionals by assisting with learning and automating routine tasks
objection: Relying on AI for learning and decision-making can weaken critical thinking, because students and adults may stop evaluating sources, spotting errors, and reasoning independently, leading to overreliance on fluent but unverified answers.

target: AG1's claim that AI can expand accessibility and help marginalized groups
objection: AI systems trained on biased data can reproduce and amplify racism and discrimination, so the same tools that claim to help marginalized groups can also exclude, misclassify, or disadvantage them.

target: AG1's claim that AI can be implemented responsibly with privacy protections
objection: AI often requires large-scale collection of sensitive data such as text, voice, images, location, and behavior patterns, and business incentives for data harvesting and surveillance frequently conflict with real privacy protection.

target: AG1's example of AI improving workplace safety through monitoring risks
objection: Workplace safety monitoring can easily become general worker surveillance, increasing stress and discouraging reporting, especially when oversight and accountability are weak.

target: AG1's claim that harms from AI are mainly engineering and policy problems that can be mitigated
objection: Safeguards are unreliable in practice because incentives push companies to collect more data and deploy faster, while regulations lag behind rapidly changing models and use cases; therefore, mitigation is not a strong reason to call AI socially good overall.

target: AG1's claim that fairness audits, bias reduction, and privacy-preserving techniques can sufficiently control AI harms
objection: Bias and privacy trade-offs are not clean: fairness and privacy safeguards often reduce performance or require expensive governance, so organizations under competitive pressure will tend to accept residual bias and more data collection rather than fully protecting people.

target: AG1's claim that workplace safety monitoring can be limited and accountable
objection: Safety monitoring predictably expands into broader surveillance and productivity tracking; without strong enforceable worker control, the scope of monitoring tends to grow beyond its original purpose.

target: AG1's claim that enforceable governance can make AI socially beneficial
objection: In practice, enforcement is hard to sustain at scale because regulators lack technical capacity and real-time access, vendors keep systems proprietary and changing, and the gap between policy and deployment widens.

target: AG1's claim that AI can be net good if harms are managed
objection: The burdens of AI harm fall on individuals rather than companies: people must prove discrimination, appeal decisions, or seek remedies, while firms capture benefits immediately; this asymmetry undermines the claim that AI is socially good overall.

target: AG1's assumption that AI is not inherently power-concentrating and can be balanced by policy
objection: AI tends to concentrate power in large firms that control data, compute, distribution, and model IP, squeezing smaller businesses that cannot match compliance costs or technical infrastructure.

target: AG1's claim that transparency, liability, and audit logs can make AI deployments verifiable
objection: Meaningful verification is structurally blocked because modern AI is often proprietary and opaque, and audit logs may only reflect what companies choose to record, making compliance checks superficial.

target: AG1's claim that harms can be corrected through appeals and recourse
objection: Many AI harms are subtle, cumulative, and hard to trace to a single output, so even when appeals exist it is often not feasible to prove causation or reverse the underlying harm.

target: AG1's selective-deployment approach to making AI net beneficial
objection: Even lower-risk, ostensibly helpful AI uses still scale privacy and bias harms across millions of users, because these systems collect sensitive data and can fail more often for certain accents, languages, or groups.

target: AG1's idea that AI can be kept confined to benign uses through risk-tiering
objection: Scope creep is predictable: systems introduced as conveniences often become decision-support, enforcement, or behavioral-tracking tools over time, so boundaries are not stable in practice.

target: AG1's claim that human-in-the-loop design can prevent overreliance and preserve critical thinking
objection: Human oversight does not fully solve the problem because people still defer to fluent AI outputs, audits are incomplete, and harms remain hard to detect when causation is unclear.

target: AG1's claim that deployment gates and contractual restrictions can keep AI uses low risk
objection: Those gates fail when models drift, are updated, or acquire new integrations over time; a system that is low risk at launch can become higher risk later without the original controls covering the new behavior.

target: AG1's claim that use-case licensing and API controls can prevent misuse
objection: Downstream misuse is hard to track because AI is embedded into products and workflows across organizations, and vendors cannot realistically enforce every subtle shift from decision support into de facto decision-making.

target: AG1's claim that prompting users to verify outputs restores critical thinking
objection: Verification prompts do not restore real reasoning for most users, because many students and time-pressured adults lack the time or expertise to evaluate citations and will still offload thinking to the AI.

target: AG1's claim that lifecycle governance such as versioning, regression tests, and rollback can keep AI safe over time
objection: Rollback cannot reliably undo harms that happen before detection, such as privacy leaks, biased hiring or lending decisions, or wrongly denied services, so lifecycle controls do not erase the underlying losses.

target: AG1's claim that compliance-heavy AI governance can be broadly beneficial
objection: The cost and complexity of lifecycle controls, audit logging, and constrained deployment favor large firms with the resources to comply, which concentrates power rather than producing a general societal benefit.

target: AG1's claim that thinking scaffolds and verification prompts will solve cognitive offloading
objection: Even with better prompts, most users will not have the time or expertise to properly evaluate AI outputs, so cognitive offloading at scale remains the likely outcome.
